nameStory: This fungus gets its unusual name from its target: the catkins of alder trees, which hang down like little tongues from the branches. When the fungus infects these 'tongues,' it transforms them into swollen, distorted galls that look quite different from normal alder catkins.
description: Eastern American alder tongue gall fungus is a specialized plant pathogen that creates distinctive swollen growths on alder tree catkins. Instead of the normal, slender hanging catkins you'd expect to see, infected trees develop enlarged, bulbous structures that can be several times thicker than healthy catkins. These galls are typically yellowish to reddish-brown and have a somewhat waxy or smooth appearance. The fungus is microscopic itself, but its effects on the tree are quite visible and dramatic.

idTips.label: Swollen catkins
idTips.description: Look for alder catkins that are abnormally thick and bulbous, often 3-4 times wider than normal catkins, with a smooth, waxy surface that feels firm to the touch

idTips.label: Color change
idTips.description: Infected catkins turn yellowish, orange, or reddish-brown instead of the typical brown or green of healthy catkins

idTips.label: Persistent hanging
idTips.description: Galled catkins often remain attached to branches longer than normal catkins, which usually drop fairly quickly

idTips.label: Host tree identification
idTips.description: Only found on alder trees, which have oval leaves with prominent veins and grow in wet areas near streams and marshes

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: The galls feel dense and somewhat rubbery when gently squeezed, quite different from the papery feel of normal catkins

habitat: Found exclusively on various alder species throughout New England's wetlands, stream edges, and marshy areas. Look for it in the same moist, rich soils where alders naturally thrive - along brooks, pond margins, and in wet meadows from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Galls are most noticeable as catkins develop and the swelling becomes apparent. This is the best time to spot fresh infections as the contrast with normal catkins is most obvious.
seasonality.summer: Established galls continue to be visible and may become more pronounced in color. The waxy surface becomes more evident during warm, humid weather.
seasonality.fall: Galls often persist on trees even as normal catkins have dropped, making them easier to spot against bare or sparsely leaved branches.
seasonality.winter: Some galls may remain attached and visible on bare branches, appearing as unusual bumpy growths where catkins would normally be absent.

funFact: This fungus essentially hijacks the alder's reproductive system, turning what should be pollen-producing male catkins into fungal nurseries - it's like the fungus has convinced the tree to raise its babies instead of its own!
confusionNotes: The swollen galls might initially be mistaken for insect galls or other plant growths, but the location specifically on alder catkins (not leaves or stems) and the characteristic waxy texture help distinguish them. Remember: if it's a weird, thick catkin on an alder, it's probably this fungus.
contextualKnowledge: Like other Taphrina fungi, this species represents an ancient group of plant pathogens that have co-evolved with their hosts for millions of years. The name 'Taphrina' comes from Greek meaning 'small trench,' referring to the way these fungi create depressions in plant tissue at the microscopic level.
compareHints: Unlike Oak Leaf Blister which creates bubble-like distortions on oak leaves, or Peach Leaf Curl which causes dramatic leaf curling, this Taphrina species specifically targets the reproductive structures (catkins) rather than leaves. This makes it unique among the common Taphrina species in New England, most of which affect leaf tissue rather than flowers or catkins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Oak Leaf Blister is most closely related to Peach Leaf Curl fungus, and the two are nearly identical under a microscope.
